opening.headline: When the classification API returns a different response every time to the same input, we will cover how to determine whether instructions or examples should be changed.
body: I created an emotion classification API, and sometimes a positive word is returned, and sometimes a single sentence is returned. The post-processing code assumes that the entire response is a single label, so even a single deviation will result in an error. In times like this, many people first reach for longer instructional sentences.

This lesson distinguishes between two tools for prompts: System instructions determine the roles and rules the model will follow in every request, and few-shot examples show what the output should look like and decision patterns. We take a look at what problems each of the two tools are suitable for, and what happens when the two are mismatched.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the role of system instructions and few-shot examples
You can distinguish between problems to be solved by instructions and problems to be solved by examples.

screens.title: Same input, but the response is different every time.
screens.lead: First, read the three classification API call records. I read thinking about how the responses differ and where my post-processing code might fail.

visual.alt: A shot of three responses to the same review, with error indications from the post-processed code placed above and below.
labels: Request 2 Response: The emotion is positive.
Request 3 Response: Positive — I like the product

paragraphs: There is an API that classifies the sentiment of review sentences. I sent the same type of input, the first response was `positive`, the second response was ‘The sentiment is positive’, and the third response was ‘Positive — I like the product’. Not all answers are wrong, but they look different.

The post-processing code that receives the response from this API was created assuming that the entire response is a single word label. So only the first response passes, but the second and third responses give an error. Even if the content is correct, if the shape is different, the program cannot use the response.

When you encounter a problem like this, you may want to write longer instruction sentences or add stronger expressions. But telling a model what to do and telling it what the result should look like are two different things. This class starts from that difference.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Would it be better if I wrote longer instructions or showed an example? By the end of class, you will be able to answer this question with evidence.

screens.outro: First, let’s start by thinking about your habit of modifying your prompts.

screens.title: What do I change first when fixing a prompt?
screens.lead: As you select each habit, the instructor's thoughts unfold. Since you will not be required to enter or submit an answer, first think about which side your habits are closer to and then click.

items.prompt: Habit 1: Add strong expressions like ‘must’ and ‘absolutely’
items.answer: Strong language can signal importance, but it doesn't tell you what the results should look like. It has limited effectiveness for problems with mixed spelling or sentence structure. In this class, we establish standards for which tools should be used for which problems.

items.prompt: Habit 2: Add one more rule statement
items.answer: Adding rules is appropriate for determining behavior that the model must follow. For example, there are rules about not adding greetings or using personal information. However, as the number of rules increases, they may collide with each other or become buried, so if you try to solve every problem by adding more rules, the instructions will become longer and longer.

items.prompt: Habit 3: Attach one or two examples of desired output
items.answer: Examples are the most direct way to show at a glance what the output will look like and what the judgment patterns will look like. However, if you add examples haphazardly, you may end up following unintended patterns. The criteria for choosing an example are covered in the screen that follows.

screens.outro: Now that I have remembered my habits, let's first check what the system instructions are responsible for.

screens.title: System instructions: rules and roles for the model to follow
screens.lead: Select each tab to see where the three providers place their instructions. Compare how each method conveys the same rule: answering with only one word for the label.

tabs.label: OpenAI
tabs.body: OpenAI gives higher-level instructions through the `instructions` parameter or the `developer` message. `instructions` takes precedence over the prompt contained in `input`. The document likens the `developer` message to a function definition and the `user` message to arguments passed to that function. Label rules are written in `instructions`, such as “Reply the review’s sentiment with only one word among positive, negative, and neutral,” and the reviews to be classified are placed in `input`.

tabs.label: Gemini
tabs.body: Gemini sets the model's behavior with the `system_instruction` parameter. In the example in the document, instructions for the model to assume the role of Neko the cat are placed here. If you put a label rule in the same place, the rule will be applied to all requests even if user input changes. Content that does not vary from request to request, such as role and tone, is appropriate here.

tabs.label: Claude
tabs.body: There are no messages in role `system` in the Claude Messages API. Instead, place the `system` parameter at the top of the request and write down the roles and rules. The `messages` array contains only the conversation between the user and the model. If you write down a label rule in `system`, this rule becomes a common instruction that applies throughout the conversation.

tabs.label: common principles
tabs.body: The three methods only have different names, but their roles are the same. System instructions contain information that is common to all requests, such as role, tone, goals, and rules to follow. Conversely, input required only for this request is placed in the user message. Instructions are a tool for determining what the model should do, and other tools are better suited for determining the exact shape of the output.

screens.outro: Now that we've identified where the instructions are placed, let's see how the examples fill in the gaps where the instructions alone are lacking.

screens.title: A few-shot example: How to demonstrate formats and patterns
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare how the response to the same input changes. Notice the difference between prompts without examples and prompts with examples.

states.label: No example (zero-shot)
states.body: The prompt only tells you to "categorize the sentiment of the review" and doesn't provide any examples. This method is called zero-shot. If you send the same review, "Delivery was fast, but packaging was disappointing," the model may not know how to respond, so she may reply with an explanatory sentence, such as "Overall, I'm close to neutral. Delivery was positive, but packaging was disappointing." This is what causes the response shape to fluctuate from request to request.

states.label: 3 examples (few-shot)
states.body: Add three pairs of inputs and expected outputs under the same instructions. For example, “I really liked it” is positive, “I used it twice and it broke” is negative, and “delivery was fast, but the packaging was disappointing” is neutral. This method of containing a few examples is called few-shot. The Gemini Guide explains that examples are often used to control form, expression, scope, and overall pattern. Now the response is anchored to a single word label. Instruct students to shorten some of the instructional sentences if the example is clear enough. Claude's guide recommends wrapping examples with the tag `<example>` to separate them from instructions.

screens.outro: Now that we've established the power of examples to anchor format, let's look at the criteria for which examples are good examples.

screens.title: Diversity of examples and conflict between instructions and examples
screens.lead: Select the item title to expand it. We sequentially check the criteria for a good example and two cases where the example actually creates problems.

items.title: Three criteria for a good example
items.body: Claude Guide uses three criteria for examples: Relevant, Diverse, and Structured. Relevance means picking inputs that are similar to actual usage situations. Diversity means showing different cases evenly. Structuring involves dividing examples and instructions into categories such as the `<example>` tag to avoid confusing the model.

items.title: Insufficient examples create unintended patterns
items.body: If the example is biased to one side, the model will even follow unintended patterns. For example, if all three examples are positive, it is easy to answer positive to the negative input. So, you need to include positive, negative, and ambiguous cases evenly. Including edge cases like ambiguous reviews or empty inputs in your examples helps the model understand the boundaries.

items.title: When instructions and examples are inconsistent
items.body: Let's say the instructions say, "Answer with one word on the label," but the example is in the form of a reason, such as "Affirmative - I like the product." The model doesn't know which one to follow, making its response unstable. OpenAI's inference model guide also warns that examples must closely match the prompt instructions, and any deviation may result in poor quality. The fix is ​​to match the output shape of the instructions and examples to one.

screens.outro: Now, let's look at the symptoms and organize the criteria for deciding whether to solve the problem with instructions or examples.

screens.title: Explanation: Problems to be solved with instructions and problems to be solved with examples
screens.lead: Read the table from top to bottom and follow which tool the instructor selects for each symptom. The key is to first ask whether the symptom is a rule violation or a cosmetic problem.

data.caption: Judgment by symptom: Solve with instructions or examples?
rows: A greeting is added before the answer.
Write “print only labels” in the system instructions.
Attach input/output pairs that show the correct label shape.
Customer personal information should not be included in the summary.
Set a rule not to use personal information in system instructions
Judgment standards for ambiguous reviews are shaken
Examples of boundary-spanning cases are provided.
An instruction is one word, but an example is a sentence with a reason.
Match the output shape of instructions and examples to one
data.notes: The key distinction is simple. Instructions determine what should or should not be done. We provide examples of what the results look like and how to determine ambiguous cases. When using two tools together, you should check them at the end to see if they have the same shape. The habit of choosing one tool per symptom makes it clear what each tool does and avoids unnecessarily long prompts. It also serves as a standard to know where to start when the same symptoms appear again. This habit prevents unnecessarily long prompts.

screens.outro: Now that we have established the classification criteria, let us solve the actual case step by step.

screens.title: Commentary: Case where the response format of the classification API is unstable
screens.lead: The instructor explains the first case step by step. Select the right arrow to advance to the next step and see how the prompt changes.

steps.title: Check current status
steps.body: Right now the prompt is just one line: “Categorize the sentiment of the review.” In this state, the response is a mixture of word and sentence types, and the post-processing code produces an error in the sentence type response.

steps.title: cause determination
steps.body: First, we consider whether the model broke the rules or did not know the shape. Nowhere in the instructions is there a need for a prohibitive rule such as “don’t use a salutation.” The model just hasn't yet seen what the output should look like, so this is a format issue.

steps.title: Add example
steps.body: Wrap three input/output pairs, each containing positive, negative, and ambiguous reviews, with the tag `<examples>`. For example, “I really like it” shows `positive`, “I used it twice and it broke” shows `negative`, and “delivery was fast, but the packaging was disappointing” shows `neutral`. Check for diversity to avoid containing only one-sided results.

steps.title: collision check
steps.body: Make sure that the “print only labels” instruction and the output shape in the example match each other. If the instructions say one word and the example is accompanied by a reason explanation, the model will falter. This step is to visually compare the two shapes to see if they both label the same word.

steps.title: Check results
steps.body: After modification, the response is fixed to a single word label and the post-processing code works as is. In summary, rule problems were solved with instructions, shape problems were solved with examples, and at the end, it was checked to see if there was any discrepancy between the two.

screens.outro: Now that I have finished the explanation, I will close the class by summarizing the key points.

screens.title: Key takeaway: Rules are instructions, formats are examples.
screens.lead: We summarize the flow of this class in one step. Check the answer to the question posed at the beginning: whether to write long instructions or show examples.

paragraphs: Answering the initial question, the problem of mixing up response shapes is usually solved with examples. Post-processing code is broken not because the model breaks a rule, but because it has never seen what the result should look like. No matter how long the instructions are, the exact shape will not be conveyed.

System instructions contain elements common to all requests, such as role, tone, goals, and rules to follow. OpenAI delivers this instruction with the `instructions` or `developer` message, Gemini uses `system_instruction`, and Claude uses the top-level `system` parameter. On the other hand, few-shot examples fix the format and decision pattern by showing pairs of inputs and expected outputs.

Good examples are relevant, varied, and structured. If the example is biased to one side, it creates an unintended pattern, and if the instructions and examples are misaligned, the response becomes unstable. Therefore, when fixing a prompt, it is best to first distinguish whether the symptom is a rule problem or a shape problem, and then check the instructions and examples together after fixing it.

This order will keep your prompts from being unnecessarily long and make it easier to track how changes you make will change the response. In summary, the criteria for judging this class are three steps: first read the nature of the symptom, select the appropriate tool, and finally compare the two. The first thing to do when the shape of your response falters is not to increase the instructions, but to create a pair of accurate output examples.

callout.label: distinction to remember
callout.text: What to do is indicated by instructions and what the result will look like by examples.

glossary.def: High-level instructions that contain the role, tone, and rules the model will follow in all requests. Depending on the provider, it is passed as instructions, system_instruction, and system parameters.
This is a method that shows the format and pattern of the output by showing several pairs of input and expected output. A method without examples is called zero-shot.
This is a property that prevents the model from following unintended patterns by evenly including different examples and edge cases.
This is a state in which the output shape of the instruction sentence and the example are different, making it unstable which one the model will follow.

misconceptions.myth: The longer and stronger the rule, the more fixed the response format.
misconceptions.fact: The format is communicated more clearly by showing examples of input and output rather than explaining it in sentences. Strong expressions do not add information about shape.
Relevance and variety are more important than quantity. If the examples all show the same result, the model will apply the pattern to places you didn't intend.

misconceptions.myth: Even if instructions and examples are used separately, they do not affect each other.
misconceptions.fact: If the two are misaligned, the model cannot tell which side to follow, so the response is shaky. Instructions and examples should always fit together.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Rules are fixed as instructions, and formats are fixed as examples.
System instructions contain roles and rules that are common to all requests, and are delivered at different locations for each provider.
Good examples are relevant, varied, structured, and separate from instructions.
If the instructions and examples are mismatched, the response may become unstable, so check them together.

checks.q: The classification API alternates between the labels `positive`, `Positive`, and `favorable`. Which change best addresses this inconsistency?
options: Write strongly by adding ‘must’ or ‘absolute’ to directive sentences.
Attach input/output example pairs that show the correct output shape.
Write more rules by lengthening the system instructions
Repeat the same request once more in the user message
checks.explain: In this example, inconsistent spelling and presentation indicate that the output format is not sufficiently specified. Input-output examples demonstrate the exact format and pattern the model should follow.

wrong.0: Strong expressions do not tell you what the output will look like.
wrong.2: Writing more rules doesn't convey the exact shape.
wrong.3: Request iteration does not add format information.

checks.explain: A zero-shot is a prompt with no examples, and a few-shot is a prompt with a few examples. System instructions create common rules, and examples without variety create unintended patterns.
